## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}

\end{marginfigure}

![](images/svg/margin_stack.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Fleet Machine Learning Systems Stack"}

*Fleet stack focus for this chapter.*

_Why must the unit of machine learning systems design become the fleet rather than the model?_

Machine learning at fleet scale is judged by the whole system, and a local improvement can move cost into a layer that its designer did not measure. Faster computation can expose a network bottleneck; larger jobs can lose more work to failure; a service that meets latency targets can still lack evidence required for deployment. The model remains central, but its accuracy and execution speed do not determine whether the complete system delivers useful work. Adding accelerators is therefore a design decision about shared resources and obligations, not simply a purchase of more arithmetic. If communication and recovery consume the saved execution time, the expansion can increase cost without improving progress. If the resulting service cannot preserve availability or account for its effects on users, successful training does not establish readiness for deployment. Single-node reasoning remains necessary because every participant still has local limits, but it cannot settle decisions whose consequences cross machines, teams, and operating boundaries. The engineering responsibility is to connect those consequences before accepting the design. That requires evidence about what improves, what becomes more constrained, and who owns the costs transferred elsewhere. A defensible decision may expand the fleet, change how work is distributed, or postpone release until the operating requirements can be met. In C³ terms, the task is to follow the binding compute, communication, or coordination constraint across layers and keep its displaced costs visible.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Distill the volume into the six principles and a constraint map for distributed ML systems
- Diagnose a fleet design's binding C³ term using measured execution costs and failure exposure
- Analyze how infrastructure, distributed training, inference, operations, and governance interact across the fleet stack
- Translate security, fairness, privacy, carbon, and reliability obligations into measurable design constraints
- Defend a fleet expansion or model-release decision using fitted scaling-law gains, operational measurements, and governance evidence

:::

## Distilling Distributed ML Systems {#sec-conclusion-synthesizing-distributed-ml-systems-bac9}

A faster accelerator can finish its local work sooner yet leave the training job waiting on the same congested collective. Scale creates qualitative change\index{Scale Moment!qualitative change} because the binding constraint can leave the node. It moves into the fabric that carries gradients, into the recovery machinery that restores state after routine failure, into the service contract that decides whether capacity reaches users in time, and into the obligations that decide whether the service may run at all. The book opened on that transition, the scale moment, and on the empirical scaling laws of @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043 that keep forcing it. Because each further reduction in loss demands a multiplicative increase in compute, demand for fleet capacity does not settle at the size where the last design worked. Each of the four parts since has answered a share of the question that transition raised by naming a constraint, the measurement that exposes it, and the mechanism that moves it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The scale moment and the qualitative shift to fleet-scale systems are established in @sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment.
:::

A frontier-model production system\index{Frontier model!fleet infrastructure} can span thousands of accelerators, with fabric links, storage tiers, schedulers, serving replicas, security controls, and governance checks supporting the same workload, and any one layer can bind the entire system: a slow checkpoint in the storage tier can waste an entire training window, a congested fabric across the interconnect can erase scaling gains from added compute, underprovisioned capacity in the serving pool can turn model quality into user-visible latency, and an unmeasured responsibility constraint can block deployment even after the technical system works. That coupling across the stack is what separates foundational ML engineering\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!single-node foundation} from distributed ML engineering\index{Distributed ML engineering!fleet stack shift}. The single-node foundation, organized by the D·A·M lens of data, algorithm, and machine, already couples models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment constraints. Distributed ML engineering extends that reasoning to shared infrastructure, distributed protocols, and governance across a fleet.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The single-machine foundation of data, algorithm, and machine is collected for reference in @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy.
:::

The physical substrate\index{Physical substrate!hardware limits}\index{Infrastructure!rates and physical limits} supplies the rates that higher layers inherit. Accelerator topology\index{Accelerator!topology}, data-loading throughput, and network contention constrain how the Distribution band\index{Fleet Stack!Distribution band} partitions, synchronizes, and recovers work. The Serving band\index{Fleet Stack!Serving band} converts that coordinated execution into a service with latency, availability, and cost obligations. The Governance band\index{Fleet Stack!Governance band} determines whether the service remains secure, robust, sustainable, and accountable. Six principles state these inherited constraints as engineering claims, in the order of the book's four parts.

## Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems {#sec-conclusion-six-principles-distributed-ml-systems-746a}

When a 16,384-GPU training job suffers an unexpected interruption every three hours or a 100-server fan-out query hits a 99th-percentile tail delay on the majority of requests, the failure comes from the fleet's physical and institutional structure rather than an operator mistake. The six engineering practices introduced with the fleet stack describe how a fleet engineer responds to those realities; the six principles of distributed ML systems\index{Distributed ML!governing principles} describe what the fleet's physical and institutional constraints make true, whatever the practice. Each condenses the part-level principles stated at the opening of its part. Part I's fleet principles condense into the first, Part II's distributed ML principles into the second and third (its empirical scaling law instead supplies the demand side of the growth decision weighed below), Part III's fleet-in-production principles into the fourth, and Part IV's responsible fleet principles into the fifth and sixth; the paragraphs below cite the part-level principles each one draws on. Each also explains why one of the practices is necessary rather than merely prudent. A fleet that loses training progress to routine interruptions must budget recovery as part of normal operation, which is why treating failure as steady state is a practice. A bottleneck that migrates whenever one term shrinks is why the engineer must expect it to move and measure the layers it moves into.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The six engineering practices, from instrument first to co-design hardware with algorithms, are established with the fleet stack in @sec-vol2-introduction-foundational-concepts.
:::

The Fleet Law, the distributed counterpart of the single-machine iron law\index{Iron law!vs. fleet law}, connects these principles to execution costs\index{Fleet law!distributed step time}\index{Fleet law!C³ taxonomy mapping}. It is the step-time equation of @eq-fleet-law, unchanged:

$$ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime $$ {#eq-conclusion-fleet-law}

Infrastructure sets the per-device rates behind $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount$ and the link bandwidths behind $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$. Communication and waiting contribute to $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$; neither is guaranteed to shrink as $\DeviceCount$ rises. Failure lands in the same terms. Checkpoint pauses, detection timeouts, and restarts add to $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ averaged over the run, asynchronous checkpointing and warm restart move part of that cost into $\OverlappedTime$, and a rollback adds the lost steps back to the work the run must still complete. Serving applies the same accounting discipline to requests, including queueing and routing delay. Responsibility and sustainability add no new term, but they spend the existing ones. Verification work occupies compute, approval gates add coordination that no replica count removes, and every second of step time costs joules at the fleet's average power. Their acceptance also requires evidence that execution time cannot supply, such as subgroup error rates, privacy accounting, and energy measured over a stated boundary.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The term-by-term decomposition of the Fleet Law is developed in @sec-appdx-c3-taxonomy-component-decomposition.
:::

Placed on the fleet stack, the six principles follow its four bands\index{Fleet Stack!layered architecture}\index{Fleet Stack!working discipline} (@fig-fleet-stack-conclusion). While the Infrastructure band determines physical capability, the Distribution band partitions execution and therefore carries both communication and failure recovery, one principle per row, whereas the Serving band bounds runtime delivery by its contract. The uppermost Governance band carries two principles that divide it by obligation rather than strictly by row: Responsibility, placed beside the Assurance row, covers every obligation owed to the people the system affects, including both the security and robustness of the Assurance row and the fairness and accountability work that @sec-responsible-ai develops in the band's top row, whereas Sustainability, placed beside that top row, covers the resource obligation alone. The arrow that runs the length of the stack marks the scale moment. Rather than acting as a seventh principle, it is the premise on which the volume opened, and crossing it is what turns each of the six from a local concern into a fleet-wide constraint.

::: {#fig-fleet-stack-conclusion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Fleet Stack Revisited**: The eight rows and four bands of @fig-fleet-stack, redrawn as the territory each of the six principles governs, with its key metric from @tbl-vol2-principles. The Infrastructure and Serving principles each own a whole band, and the Distribution band carries one principle per row. The Governance band divides by obligation rather than by row: Responsibility covers the Assurance row and the governance half of the top row, while Sustainability covers the resource half. The arrow runs the length of the stack because scale changes the behavior of every band." fig-alt="Stack of eight rows in four bands labeled Part I Infrastructure, Part II Distribution, Part III Serving, and Part IV Governance, drawn as outlined territories. Infrastructure is one outlined region holding Facility and Accelerators and Fabric and Storage, labeled 1 infrastructure determines capability with FLOP/s, bandwidth, rack power. Distribution has two separate regions: Distributed Execution labeled 2 communication can dominate with exposed communication time, and Reliability and Control labeled 3 failure is routine with MTBF, checkpoint overhead. Serving is one region holding Runtime and Serving and Operations, labeled 4 serving is bounded by its contract with p99 latency within the SLO. In Governance the top row is split into a Governance half and a Sustainability half; an L-shaped region joins the Governance half with the Assurance row, labeled 5 responsibility constrains design with privacy budget, subgroup error, and the Sustainability half is its own region, labeled 6 sustainability is a first-order cost with energy per query, carbon. An upward arrow on the left is labeled scale creates qualitative change."}
![](images/svg/fleet-stack-conclusion.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The six principles therefore work as a decision map rather than a glossary (@tbl-vol2-principles). Each row links a principle to the question, metric, and practice an engineer uses when diagnosing a fleet-scale design, and to the part and chapters that develop it. The part order is an order of dependency, not a ranking of bottlenecks; the workload and its measurements determine which constraint binds, while the layered tiers in @fig-fleet-stack-conclusion locate the governing architectural band.

| **Principle**                            |       **Core question**        | **Key metric**                                                        | **Practice it demands**                        | **Developed in**                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------------------------|:------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Infrastructure determines capability** |       What is possible?        | FLOP/s, memory and bisection bandwidth, rack power                    | Co-design hardware with algorithms             | Part I: @sec-compute-infrastructure, @sec-network-fabrics, @sec-data-storage                         |
| **Communication can dominate**           |    What is the bottleneck?     | Exposed communication time, scaling efficiency                        | Expect bottlenecks to migrate                  | Part II: @sec-collective-communication, @sec-distributed-training-systems                            |
| **Failure is routine**                   |       How do we recover?       | MTBF, checkpoint overhead, rollback time                              | Treat failure as steady state                  | Part II: @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability, @sec-fleet-orchestration                                  |
| **Serving is bounded by its contract**   | What reaches the user in time? | ML productivity goodput, p99 latency within the SLO, cost per request | Reserve headroom for recovery and tail latency | Part III: @sec-performance-engineering, @sec-inference-scale, @sec-edge-intelligence, @sec-ops-scale |
| **Responsibility constrains design**     |        Who is affected?        | Privacy budget, subgroup error rates, audit trails                    | Instrument first                               | Part IV: @sec-security-privacy, @sec-robust-ai, @sec-responsible-ai                                  |
| **Sustainability is a first-order cost** |       What is the cost?        | kWh per training run, energy per query, carbon                        | Compound small efficiency gains                | Part IV: @sec-sustainable-ai                                                                         |

: **Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems**: The qualitative shifts that occur when ML systems move from single machines to distributed production, grouped by the part of the book that develops them. Each principle connects to a governing question, the metric that tests it, the engineering practice it makes necessary, and the chapters where the concept is developed in depth. {#tbl-vol2-principles tbl-colwidths="[20,15,20,17,28]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-scale-facts
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION SCALE FACTS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Six principles of distributed ML systems.
# │
# │ Goal: Keep local numerical claims tied to executable calculations.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — six-principles prose, fallacies, and chapter summary share scale facts.
# │ Show: p99 fan-out tail probability, Llama 3 failure cadence, cluster ratio and
# │       effective training time, straggler drop.
# │ How: Direct probability and rate calculations from the stated assumptions.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import HOURS_PER_DAY, Literature, Models, Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ConclusionScaleFacts:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tail_servers = 100
    tail_percentile = 0.99
    llama_failures = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions
    llama_days = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays
    llama_effective_fraction = Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_EffectiveTrainingTimeFraction
    hours_per_day = HOURS_PER_DAY
    straggler_speed = 0.80
    llama_gpus = Models.Language.Llama3_405B.training_accelerators_ref.magnitude
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    tail_hit_probability = 1 - tail_percentile**tail_servers
    llama_hours_per_failure = llama_days * hours_per_day / llama_failures
    straggler_drop = 1 - straggler_speed
    llama_ref_ratio = llama_gpus / ref_gpus  # Llama 3 cluster vs. reference
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(round(tail_hit_probability * 100) == 63, "Tail probability changed")
    check(3.0 < llama_hours_per_failure < 3.2, "Failure cadence changed")
    check(round(straggler_drop * 100) == 20, "Straggler throughput drop changed")
    check(llama_ref_ratio == 16, "Llama 3 cluster ratio changed")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    tail_servers_str = fmt_count(tail_servers, commas=False, label="server")
    tail_percentile_str = fmt_int(tail_percentile * 100, commas=False)
    tail_hit_pct_str = fmt_percent(tail_hit_probability, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    llama_failures_str = fmt_count(llama_failures, commas=False, label="unexpected interruption")
    llama_days_str = fmt_time(llama_days, "day", precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    llama_hours_per_failure_str = fmt_time(llama_hours_per_failure, 'hour', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    straggler_speed_pct_str = fmt_percent(straggler_speed, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    straggler_drop_pct_str = fmt_percent(straggler_drop, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    llama_gpus_str = fmt_int(llama_gpus, commas=True)
    llama_ref_ratio_str = fmt_int(llama_ref_ratio, commas=False)
    llama_effective_pct_str = fmt_percent(llama_effective_fraction, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

The first principle is that infrastructure determines capability. Physical infrastructure constrains both feasible configurations and attainable rates. Memory capacity and safe power and cooling envelopes limit how much state and active hardware a configuration can support. Cluster-wide bisection bandwidth\index{Bisection bandwidth!scaling ceiling} instead limits how quickly distributed work can exchange data (principle \ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}); insufficient bandwidth can make a deadline or cost target unattainable without making the computation impossible. Storage sets a further ceiling, because accelerators that the data pipeline cannot feed sit idle regardless of their peak rate (principle \ref{pri-io-wall}). These are the memory, network, and energy walls of the scale moment, measured at the scale of the node, the fabric, and the facility. Partitioning, batch size, and communication scheduling determine how those limits bind, and mastering the fleet requires understanding them from chip-level thermal density\index{Thermal design power!hardware limits} to cluster-wide bisection bandwidth.

The second principle is that communication can become the binding term at scale [@jiang2024megascale; @narayanan2021], with its cost set by the bandwidth-latency trade-off (principle \ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}) inside the Fleet Law's $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ term. Communication intensity, the ratio of bytes crossing the network to local FLOPs, indicates network demand relative to arithmetic. Whether that demand dominates also depends on achieved compute and network rates, message sizes, topology, and overlap. Gradient synchronization\index{Gradient synchronization!communication bottleneck} and straggler effects\index{Straggler!barrier latency} must therefore be measured on the synchronous step's critical path rather than inferred from byte volume alone.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The communication-intensity ratio is established in @sec-vol2-introduction-ci-ratio.
:::

Collective communication algorithms, including Ring AllReduce,[^fn-ring-allreduce-collective] popularized for deep learning by Horovod [@sergeev2018horovod], gradient compression, and overlapping computation with communication\index{Communication overlap!collective hiding}, address communication bottlenecks. For dense collective workloads, conventional oversubscribed fabrics often bottleneck, motivating high-bisection fabrics\index{Bisection bandwidth!network fabric} and transport choices matched to ML communication patterns. Recognizing when communication is the active constraint clarifies when algorithmic optimizations will help and when they merely shift work between equally constrained resources, the displacement of overhead (principle \ref{pri-conservation-overhead}) that makes bottlenecks migrate. Expanding the fabric across thousands of nodes also multiplies the components that a job needs at the same instant, and that multiplication makes failure routine.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Ring collectives, communication overlap, and gradient compression are established in @sec-collective-communication.
:::

[^fn-ring-allreduce-collective]: **Ring AllReduce**\index{Ring AllReduce!bandwidth optimality}: A collective that sends $2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount$ bytes per worker and receives the same amount for message size $\CollectivePayloadSize$, giving $\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency + \frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}$ under the $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ communication model, with $\LinkBandwidth$ denoting bandwidth in each full-duplex direction. The coefficient approaches 2$\times$ message volume per worker as $\DeviceCount$ grows, while remaining bandwidth-optimal for large messages.

The third principle is that failure is routine. A job that needs many components at once can encounter interruptions frequently enough that recovery becomes normal operation. The reliability gap\index{Reliability gap!routine failure} in @sec-vol2-introduction-reliability-gap follows from @eq-reliability-gap, under which a job that needs every one of its components at once, each independently available with probability $\ComponentAvailability$, sees its availability decay exponentially in the number of components it requires. Meta's experience training Llama 3\index{Llama 3!failure cadence} on `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_gpus_str` GPUs, `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_ref_ratio_str` times the Archetype A reference cluster, documented `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_failures_str` over `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_days_str`, averaging one unexpected interruption every `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_hours_per_failure_str` [@dubey2024llama]. A failed rank can stall every other rank in its collective. Under full-job checkpoint recovery, the affected job rolls back to its last checkpoint; other jobs in the fleet need not roll back. For a fixed amount of lost wall-clock progress, wasted accelerator-time grows with the size of the affected job, which is why checkpoint cadence\index{Checkpointing!cadence and recovery} and recovery architecture are first-order design dimensions.

Architects must embed failure handling from the beginning. Checkpointing strategies\index{Checkpointing!overhead trade-off} balance write overhead against expected lost work, and the Young-Daly interval (principle \ref{pri-young-daly}) estimates that balance under its failure and checkpoint-cost assumptions. Elastic training\index{Elastic training!dynamic membership} supports changing cluster membership, while graceful degradation\index{Graceful degradation!service availability} preserves a defined level of service as capacity diminishes. Each mechanism needs a tested recovery contract; its name alone does not establish that progress or service quality survives a failure. Recovery should automate known failure paths and escalate cases whose safe response requires investigation. Recovery also needs capacity. A restarted synchronous job makes progress only when the scheduler can again grant it an atomic, topology-feasible gang allocation (principle \ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}), which is why fleet orchestration keeps spare capacity, preempts lower-priority work, and admits only allocations a job can actually use. Coordination, the third C³ axis, is not confined to this principle. It is paid in recovery and gang scheduling here, in request routing for serving, and in the approval gates of governance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Checkpoint cadence, mean time between failures (MTBF) analysis, and elastic recovery protocols are established in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability.
:::

Communication and failure together constitute the operational reality of the Distribution band. Deployment carries both into a setting where the unit of work is a user request rather than a training step, which gives the fourth principle, that serving is bounded by its contract\index{Service contract!useful capacity}. The accounting begins before any request arrives. The ML goodput decomposition (principle \ref{pri-ml-goodput}) assigns each interval of capacity that the built fleet loses to exactly one of its three factors (scheduling, runtime, or program goodput), so that every loss has one owner. A serving fleet's useful capacity is then the work it completes within its latency, availability, and cost targets, not the work its accelerators execute in isolation, which is what @sec-inference-scale-serving-tax-overhead-distribution-5ef3 measures as service-level objective (SLO) goodput. Production inference that waits for every worker in a fan-out inherits tail effects [@dean2013], because completion depends on the slowest required response. A request that touches `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_servers_str` has a `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_hit_pct_str` chance that at least one of them responds beyond its `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_percentile_str`th-percentile latency when server delays are independent,[^fn-tail-effect-latency] so a latency that is rare for one server becomes the common case for the request. Routing is where coordination enters the request path. Probing two of $\ReplicaCount$ replicas and sending the request to the less loaded (principle \ref{pri-power-two-choices}) sharply shortens the longest queue in the idealized balls-into-bins model, at the cost of only two probes. On live traffic the gain still depends on arrivals, service times, and how fresh the load estimate is, so it narrows the tail rather than bounding every request's latency.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The power of two choices and the queue-length bounds behind it are established in @sec-inference-scale-power-two-choices-ffdd.
:::

[^fn-tail-effect-latency]: **Tail latency**\index{Tail latency!fan-out probability}: The estimate is one minus the probability that every server answers within its own percentile, which under independence is the per-server probability raised to the number of servers; @sec-inference-scale-load-balancing-request-routing-4997 analyzes the tail effects it summarizes. Shared congestion correlates server delays, so a real fleet can sit above or below this figure, and the independence assumption has to be checked against measured traces.

Inside each replica, the memory wall\index{Memory wall} returns as a serving constraint. Compute (TFLOP/s) can be abundant while memory bandwidth (GB/s) gates small-batch autoregressive decode\index{Decode bottleneck} (principle \ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}), because weight and KV-cache traffic from high-bandwidth memory (HBM)\index{HBM!decode bandwidth} leaves compute units underused. Batching amortizes weight reads across output tokens, so the binding constraint can shift toward compute, KV traffic, or the latency budget; a replica's execution envelope must therefore be measured before any fleet-level policy is chosen. The contract also has a lifetime. A heavily used model can spend more on inference than it did on training (principle \ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}), so the cost per request, not the one-time training bill, eventually dominates what the model costs to own.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_conclusion_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Schematic roofline with a small-batch decode point on the memory-bandwidth slope below the compute ceiling."}

*Small-batch decode can sit left of the roofline ridge.*
:::

Beyond the data center, the contract takes other forms. On a phone-class device the contract is the device's own power, thermal, and foreground-latency envelope, and the device enforces it by admitting background work, including local adaptation, only when the envelope has room. That admission policy has a consequence that reaches back into training. Only devices whose policy accepts the work take part in adaptation, so the serving-side contract also decides whose data the shared model learns from (principle \ref{pri-participation-selects-population}), a bias the fifth principle must then account for. Across a platform of hundreds of models, staged rollouts and per-service reliability budgets enforce the contract release by release, so every release must carry evidence that its targets still hold. Once the fleet can deliver a service, governance determines whether it is allowed to.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ On-device adaptation within phone-class power and thermal envelopes is established in @sec-edge-intelligence-energy-thermal-constraint-analysis-3133.
:::

The fifth principle is that responsibility constrains design. Responsible AI\index{Responsible AI!engineering constraints} translates risk-management frameworks into engineering constraints [@nist2023airmf]. Safety-specific risks such as reward hacking\index{Reward hacking!safety risk}, distribution shift, and scalable oversight show why those constraints need implementation mechanisms [@amodei2016concrete]. Fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and safety are first-class requirements that shape system architecture throughout the ML lifecycle. The part-level principles behind this one span provenance, because a model can be trusted only as far as the verified record of its data, code, and weights reaches (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}); privacy, because released outputs can disclose what a model learned (principle \ref{pri-information-leakage}); robustness, whose evaluation and defenses require mechanism-specific resource budgets (principle \ref{pri-robustness-compute-penalty}); and feedback, because deployed decisions can shape future training observations (principle \ref{pri-sociotechnical-feedback}).

The fairness impossibility theorem\index{Fairness impossibility theorem} (principle \ref{pri-fairness-impossibility}) shows why some requirements cannot be satisfied by tuning alone. With unequal base rates and imperfect prediction, a risk score cannot be both calibrated within each group and balanced across groups within each outcome class [@kleinberg2016inherent], the score-level counterpart of the conflict between equal opportunity and demographic parity in the admissions example of @sec-responsible-ai-fairness-criteria-conflict. The deployment therefore needs justified criteria, evidence that they hold, and an owner authorized to respond when they fail. Monitoring exposes supported disparities but cannot choose the criterion or provide a remedy by itself. These obligations belong in the design alongside performance requirements, which is why the practice this principle demands is to instrument first. Subgroup error rates, privacy accounting, and audit trails must be collected before the decision they are meant to justify, because a disparity that was never measured cannot be detected, attributed, or remedied after deployment. Environmental responsibility extends the Governance band into the physical resource budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The calibration and score-balance conditions that the fairness impossibility theorem relates are established in @sec-responsible-ai-fairness-criteria-conflict.
:::

The sixth principle is that sustainability\index{Sustainable infrastructure!first-order cost} is a first-order cost. Environmental impact of large-scale ML\index{Sustainable infrastructure!carbon footprint} elevates resource efficiency to a primary engineering constraint [@strubell2019; @patterson2021carbon]. The energy-scale invariant of @sec-introduction-energyscale-invariant-a0d6 supplies the accounting discipline, a fixed boundary for useful work and for the energy it consumes, and the Fleet Law explains why exposed communication and synchronization cost joules as well as seconds, since a step's energy is approximately its average power times $\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)$. The Jevons paradox of AI\index{Jevons paradox!rebound effect} adapts Jevons's resource-efficiency argument [@jevons1865coal] to explain why hardware efficiency gains alone do not eliminate power and carbon costs (principle \ref{pri-jevons-paradox}). Cheaper computation can expand deployment, so usage growth can offset per-query savings. An absolute carbon budget\index{Carbon budget!fleet constraint} bounds emissions only when accounting and admission decisions enforce it over the stated lifecycle and time horizon.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Carbon accounting, energy metrics, and Jevons rebound effects are established in @sec-sustainable-ai.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-sustainability-anchors
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION SUSTAINABILITY ANCHORS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Sixth-principle paragraph on the carbon accounting chain.
# │
# │ Goal: Recall the sustainability chapter's two anchors from the registry.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — sixth-principle accounting-chain paragraph only.
# │ Show: GPT-3 ≈ 1,287 MWh ≈ 120 US household-years; Poland/Quebec grid
# │       carbon intensity ≈ 41x.
# │ How: training energy / household annual electricity; ratio of grid
# │      intensities (equals the carbon ratio at fixed energy).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure, Models, ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.core.units import MWh
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_energy, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_energy = Models.Language.GPT3.training_energy_mwh
    household_energy = ReferenceStats.EnergyAnchors.USHouseholdAnnualElectricity
    quebec_g_kwh = float(Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec.carbon_intensity_g_kwh)
    poland_g_kwh = float(Infrastructure.Grids.Poland.carbon_intensity_g_kwh)
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    household_years = (gpt3_energy / household_energy).to("").magnitude
    grid_ratio = poland_g_kwh / quebec_g_kwh
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(119 <= household_years <= 121, "GPT-3 household-year anchor changed")
    check(40 < grid_ratio < 42, "Poland/Quebec grid ratio changed")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_mwh_str = fmt_energy(gpt3_energy, unit=MWh, precision=0, commas=True)
    household_years_str = fmt_int(round(household_years), commas=False)
    grid_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(grid_ratio, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Sustainability thus becomes an engineering discipline with its own accounting chain, in which IT energy scaled by the facility's power usage effectiveness and the grid's carbon intensity gives operational emissions, and the embodied carbon of manufacturing the hardware joins the total. Two links show how far the chain can swing. Training GPT-3 consumed about `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.gpt3_mwh_str`, roughly `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.household_years_str` US household-years of electricity [@li2020estimating], and the same energy drawn from Poland's coal-heavy grid emits about `{python} ConclusionSustainabilityAnchors.grid_ratio_mult_str` the carbon it would on Quebec's hydroelectric grid. The chain also explains the practice this principle demands. Small efficiency gains compound across every accelerator and every query in the fleet, but usage growth can absorb them, so compounding efficiency bounds total emissions only when an absolute budget caps the total. Carbon-aware scheduling\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!fleet placement}, lifecycle assessment,[^fn-lifecycle-assessment-sustainability] and efficiency optimization are the engineering means of meeting that budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operational and embodied carbon calculation is established in @sec-sustainable-ai-carbon-footprint-calculation-c2fe.
:::

[^fn-lifecycle-assessment-sustainability]: **Lifecycle assessment**\index{Lifecycle assessment}: @Sec-sustainable-ai-hardware-lifecycle-environmental-assessment-66ee evaluates environmental impact across a system's lifespan, including embodied carbon\index{Embodied carbon!hardware lifecycle} from hardware manufacturing. Embodied emissions can become a substantial share of total impact on clean grids or when hardware is lightly used.

The six principles describe the qualitative change\index{Scale Moment!production behavior} that scale can produce, and the scaling laws (principle \ref{pri-universal-scaling}) keep carrying a team that pursues lower loss into regimes its previous fleet never exercised. Each new regime brings behavior that emerges\index{Scale Moment!emergent phenomena} from familiar mechanisms, as the scale moment first showed. A training job that scales from 8 GPUs to 8,000 can meet communication bottlenecks, load imbalance, or synchronization overhead that were negligible at 8. Serving shows the same shift in its event rates. At a million requests a day, a one-in-a-million per-request failure is expected about once a day, so an event that never appears in testing becomes a routine operating condition. At that scale, stragglers\index{Straggler!throughput impact} that bottleneck clusters, network partitions\index{Network partition!distributed training} that split training, and heterogeneity across hardware generations\index{Hardware heterogeneity!fleet load balancing} that complicates load balancing become design inputs rather than anomalies.

## The Complete Production System {#sec-conclusion-complete-production-system-3885}

Doubling a 1,024-GPU frontier training cluster to 2,048 GPUs halves the ideal arithmetic time per step, but it also halves the expected interval between GPU interruptions and increases both exposed collective communication and checkpoint overhead. Scaling laws set the demand for that fleet growth and the Fleet Law (@eq-conclusion-fleet-law) sets its price, so together they say when growth pays and where it breaks. The laws estimate what growth buys; they do not oblige an organization to buy it. Scaling pays while the quality gain a fitted curve predicts justifies what the fleet charges to deliver it, and that charge moves with $\DeviceCount$ on several fronts at once. Increasing $\DeviceCount$ reduces the ideal compute term $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount$ for fixed work and unchanged per-device rates, while $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ depend on the resulting partition and schedule and carry no such guarantee. Interruption exposure also grows with $\DeviceCount$, as the expansion estimate below quantifies. Within a fixed facility, the power and cooling envelope does not grow with the job, and a successful model then pays its serving cost for as long as it runs. Growth therefore breaks on either side. On the model side, the breakdown conditions of @tbl-scaling-breakdown mark where extrapolating a fitted quality curve becomes unreliable, for example when model capacity outgrows the available tokens or added data stops supplying new information. On the systems side, the scaling wall\index{Scaling wall!fleet growth} of @sec-distributed-training-scaling-math marks where added communication and coordination consume the compute time that added accelerators save (principle \ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}), and a site's deliverable power caps the configuration regardless of how the work is partitioned. A complete production design has to evaluate both sides together.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION EXAMPLE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how doubling the Archetype A reference cluster changes failure exposure.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │ Show: 1,024 -> 2,048 GPUs; GPU-only job MTBF ≈ 48.8 h -> 24.4 h; checkpoint overhead ≈ 1.41x;
# │       10,000-GPU cluster of the full-system failure analysis.
# │ How: MTBF_job = MTTF_gpu / N; Young-Daly overhead ≈ sqrt(2·delta/MTBF_job), so it grows as sqrt(N).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class ConclusionExpansion:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    expansion_factor = 2  # scenario: double the reference cluster
    ft_cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators  # cluster of the full-system failure analysis
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    exp_gpus = ref_gpus * expansion_factor
    ref_job_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / ref_gpus
    exp_job_mtbf_h = gpu_mttf_h / exp_gpus
    # Young-Daly optimum: overhead ≈ sqrt(2·delta/MTBF_job), independent of delta as a ratio
    ckpt_overhead_growth = math.sqrt(ref_job_mtbf_h / exp_job_mtbf_h)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ref_gpus == 1024, "Reference cluster changed")
    check(abs(ckpt_overhead_growth - math.sqrt(expansion_factor)) < 1e-9, "Young-Daly scaling changed")
    check(ft_cluster_gpus > exp_gpus, "Failure-analysis cluster should exceed the expanded cluster")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ref_gpus_str = fmt_count(ref_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    exp_gpus_str = fmt_count(exp_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    ft_cluster_gpus_str = fmt_count(ft_cluster_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    gpu_mttf_str = fmt_time(gpu_mttf_h, "hour", precision=0, commas=True, style="word")
    ref_job_mtbf_str = fmt_time(ref_job_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    exp_job_mtbf_str = fmt_time(exp_job_mtbf_h, "hour", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    ckpt_overhead_growth_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ckpt_overhead_growth, precision=2, commas=False)
```

Consider Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), whose running instance in this book is a GPT-3-class dense transformer trained with mixed precision on a reference cluster of `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ref_gpus_str` and then shipped into a global serving fleet. Checkpoint bursts must land without starving the data loaders, while collective results must arrive before the computations that depend on them. Communication can overlap independent work, but its exposed remainder delays progress. At that scale, recovery planning uses observed write costs and failure rates, with the Young-Daly interval\index{Young-Daly formula!optimal interval}\index{Checkpointing!Young-Daly formula} supplying an approximation where its assumptions hold [@young1974; @daly2006]. Serving SLOs\index{SLO!headroom for recovery} require headroom for rollback and fallback, while governance controls\index{Governance!fleet constraints} enforce approved conditions on which data, models, and outputs may reach users. These are coupled rates, budgets, failure exposures, and policy constraints that must be designed before deployment.

The production system begins with physical capacity, but capacity matters only when the rates line up. Physical compute infrastructure supplies accelerators, power, cooling, and fabric; the data tier determines whether data can arrive fast enough; and collective communication determines whether workers can synchronize without turning the network into the bottleneck. These subsystems must be co-designed\index{Hardware-software co-design!storage and communication}: data ingestion must meet accelerator consumption, checkpoint writes must fit the recovery budget, and the fabric must carry the actual collective traffic. These are distinct rates; matching them to workload demand matters more than making their raw bandwidths equal.

Parallelization strategies must fit those physical rates and the expected failure pattern. Data parallelism\index{Data parallelism!trade-offs}, tensor parallelism\index{Tensor parallelism!trade-offs}, and pipeline parallelism\index{Pipeline parallelism!trade-offs} are not interchangeable templates; each changes memory pressure, communication volume, checkpointing behavior, and scheduler complexity. Hybrid strategies\index{Hybrid parallelism!systems support} become useful only when the surrounding storage, fabric, and recovery design can support the shape of the partition.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid partitioning each move memory pressure, communication volume, and the pipeline bubble is established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-parallelism-strategy-comparison-d92a.
:::

Serving adds a separate acceptance boundary. The contract of the fourth principle judges the model by its latency, availability, and cost on live traffic, whether it runs in a data center replica or on a phone-class device. Some security and robustness controls execute on the request path; others operate during training, release review, or asynchronous monitoring. Each needs an evidence and response path suited to its obligation. Training throughput therefore does not establish that a model will meet live latency, recovery, security, subgroup, and carbon requirements. A fleet expansion raises two linked decisions, whether to accept the larger training job and whether to release the model it produces, and each needs its own evidence.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion-overhead
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION OVERHEAD (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Give the Young-Daly overhead an absolute baseline and turn the
# │       expansion into a stated decision rule.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — expansion worked example only.
# │ Show: 175B checkpoint ≈ 2.45 TB, write ≈ 24.5 s; overhead ≈ 1.7% at
# │       1,024 GPUs -> ≈ 2.4% at 2,048; break-even step speedup ≈ 1.01x;
# │       accelerator-hours at ideal speedup ≈ +0.7%.
# │ How: overhead ≈ sqrt(2·T_write/MTBF_job), MTBF_job = MTTF_gpu/N (GPU-only);
# │      run time ∝ T_step/(1 − overhead), so doubling shortens the run iff
# │      speedup > (1 − o_ref)/(1 − o_exp); accelerator-hours scale by
# │      (2/speedup)·(1 − o_ref)/(1 − o_exp) ≥ that ratio.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, TB, hour, second
from mlsysim.physics import calc_checkpoint_size
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ConclusionExpansionOverhead:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_bytes = calc_checkpoint_size(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters)  # 14 B/param
    write_bw = float(Systems.Reliability.Recovery.checkpoint_write_bw_gbs) * (GB / second)
    gpu_mttf_h = float(Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours)
    ref_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # Archetype A reference cluster
    exp_gpus = 2 * ref_gpus  # scenario: double the reference cluster
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    t_write_h = (ckpt_bytes / write_bw).to(hour).magnitude
    overhead_ref = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h / (gpu_mttf_h / ref_gpus))
    overhead_exp = math.sqrt(2 * t_write_h / (gpu_mttf_h / exp_gpus))
    breakeven_speedup = (1 - overhead_ref) / (1 - overhead_exp)
    ideal_speedup = exp_gpus / ref_gpus  # ideal step speedup equals the GPU ratio
    ideal_accel_hours_extra = (exp_gpus / ref_gpus) / ideal_speedup * breakeven_speedup - 1
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ref_gpus == 1024, "Reference cluster changed")
    check(22 < t_write_h * 3600 < 27, "175B checkpoint write should be ~24.5 s")
    check(0.015 < overhead_ref < 0.018, "Reference overhead should be ~1.7%")
    check(0.022 < overhead_exp < 0.025, "Expanded overhead should be ~2.4%")
    check(1.0 < breakeven_speedup < 1.02, "Break-even speedup should be just above 1")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ckpt_tb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_bytes, unit=TB, precision=2, commas=False)
    t_write_s_str = fmt_time(t_write_h * 3600, "second", precision=1, commas=False, style="word")
    overhead_ref_pct_str = fmt_percent(overhead_ref, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    overhead_exp_pct_str = fmt_percent(overhead_exp, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    breakeven_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(breakeven_speedup, precision=2, commas=False)
    ideal_accel_hours_extra_pct_str = fmt_percent(ideal_accel_hours_extra, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: conclusion-expansion-scaling-gain
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONCLUSION EXPANSION SCALING GAIN (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Frontier-model expansion worked example in The Complete Production System.
# │
# │ Goal: Put a number on the benefit side of the expansion trade-off, the loss
# │       reduction a fitted compute scaling law predicts for doubling compute.
# │ Scope: paragraph-local — expansion worked example only.
# │ Show: Kaplan compute exponent 0.050; 2^-0.050 ≈ 0.966, a loss reduction
# │       of ≈ 3.4 percent per doubling.
# │ How: L = (C / C_c)^(-alpha_C), so doubling C multiplies L by 2^(-alpha_C).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_math, fmt_percent

class ConclusionScalingGain:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    compute_law = next(e for e in Literature.KaplanScalingLaws.entries if e["axis"] == "compute")
    alpha_compute = compute_law["alpha"]  # published fit, valid only over its studied range
    compute_multiple = 2  # scenario: double the training compute
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    loss_factor = compute_multiple ** (-alpha_compute)
    loss_reduction = 1 - loss_factor
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(alpha_compute - 0.050) < 1e-9, "Kaplan compute exponent changed")
    check(0.03 < loss_reduction < 0.04, "Doubling-compute loss reduction should be ~3.4 percent")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    neg_alpha_compute_math = fmt_math(rf"-{alpha_compute:.3f}")
    loss_factor_math = fmt_math(rf"2^{{-{alpha_compute:.3f}}} \approx {loss_factor:.3f}")
    loss_reduction_pct_str = fmt_percent(loss_reduction, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

For our frontier-model case, suppose a proposed expansion doubles the reference cluster to `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_gpus_str` while retaining the fabric and checkpoint tier. Doubling $\DeviceCount$ halves the ideal $\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount$ term for fixed work at unchanged per-device rates, so the first measurement is whether that saving survives the changes in $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$ and their overlap. The recovery side can be estimated before any measurement. Assume independent GPU failures at an identical constant rate, with each failure interrupting the job. Counting those failures alone at the registry mean time to failure (MTTF) of `{python} ConclusionExpansion.gpu_mttf_str` per GPU, the job's mean time between interruptions is that MTTF divided by $\DeviceCount$, so it falls from `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ref_job_mtbf_str` to `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_job_mtbf_str`. At the Young-Daly interval of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval, the checkpoint-and-rework overhead is about $\sqrt{2\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf}$ of wall-clock time, and @sec-fault-tolerance-young-daly shows that it therefore grows as $\sqrt{\DeviceCount}$, so doubling the cluster multiplies it by about `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ckpt_overhead_growth_mult_str`. The model's `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.ckpt_tb_str` checkpoint takes about `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.t_write_s_str` to write at the registry checkpoint bandwidth, which puts the overhead at about `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.overhead_ref_pct_str` of wall-clock time on the reference cluster and about `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.overhead_exp_pct_str` on the expanded one. These figures are optimistic. They count GPU failures alone, while switches, network interface cards, and software add interruptions of their own. The full-system analysis in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-checkpoint-interval-failure-analysis-c28d, which adds PCIe-switch and network-interface failures for a cluster of `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ft_cluster_gpus_str`, arrives at a correspondingly larger overhead from the same formula. Write contention with data loading or a changed checkpoint size would also require revising them.

These estimates still yield a decision rule. In this example, measured step time covers uninterrupted execution and excludes the checkpoint-and-rework overhead estimated separately. The retained-progress factor, the checkpoint-and-rework share of what @sec-performance-engineering-runtime-goodput calls runtime goodput, accounts for that excluded cost once; a whole-run measurement that already includes it must not receive the factor again. For fixed work, run time is proportional to $\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)/(1 - \text{overhead})$, so the larger cluster shortens the run only when its measured step-time speedup exceeds the ratio of the two retained fractions, one minus the reference overhead divided by one minus the expanded overhead. Here that break-even speedup is about `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.breakeven_speedup_mult_str`, so recovery alone does not block the expansion. Short of a superlinear speedup, however, it cannot save accelerator-hours. Accelerator-hours are the GPU count times run time, so doubling the GPUs multiplies them by twice that same ratio divided by the achieved speedup. Even at the ideal 2$\times$ speedup they rise by about `{python} ConclusionExpansionOverhead.ideal_accel_hours_extra_pct_str`, and every point of scaling efficiency lost to exposed communication raises them further. The expansion therefore buys calendar time with accelerator-hours and energy, and the communication measurement, not the recovery estimate, sets that price.

That price buys time, not quality, because the work is fixed. Quality enters the comparison only if the doubled cluster spends twice the compute instead of finishing sooner, and there the fitted scaling curve prices the gain. In the compute power law that @kaplan2020scaling fitted (charted in the scaling laws of @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043, @fig-kaplan-scaling), loss falls as compute raised to the power `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.neg_alpha_compute_math`, so doubling compute multiplies loss by `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.loss_factor_math`, a reduction of about `{python} ConclusionScalingGain.loss_reduction_pct_str`. A frontier run lies beyond the range that fit studied, so the figure shows the shape of the trade rather than this run's gain. Each doubling buys the same fractional reduction, and therefore a smaller absolute one than the doubling before it, while its price, twice the accelerator-hours plus the recovery and communication overhead above, is paid in full every time.

The release decision then applies its own test. If the resulting model fails a release gate, the affected partition, placement, capacity allocation, or release plan must be revised before the release proceeds. The constraints behind those choices can conflict. A communication optimization may increase failure exposure, sustainability requirements may restrict infrastructure choices, and governance controls may consume serving latency or capacity. The displacement of overhead\index{Displacement of overhead!cross-layer trade-offs} requires measuring those transferred costs before accepting a local speedup.

The three workloads introduced as lighthouse archetypes show that no single corner of the C$^3$ taxonomy\index{C³ taxonomy!workload archetypes}\index{C³ taxonomy!binding constraints} dominates. Each workload was first characterized by a representative binding term, and following each one up the fleet stack shows what each band, and the part of the book that develops it, added to that first characterization (@tbl-conclusion-archetype-binding-terms).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The three lighthouse archetypes, and whether each stresses compute, communication, or coordination, are established in @sec-vol2-introduction-archetypes.
:::

| **Fleet stack band**          | **Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3)**                                                                                                                                                                                        | **Archetype B (DLRM at Scale)**                                                                                                                       | **Archetype C (Federated MobileNet)**                                                                                                                                                             |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Representative C$^3$ term** | Communication, fleet-wide                                                                                                                                                                                              | Coordination, in routing and placement                                                                                                                | Local compute, within the device envelope                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Infrastructure (Part I)**   | Training state and checkpoints far exceed one accelerator's memory\index{Frontier model!collective communication}, motivating partitioning; frequent tensor-parallel collectives favor the fastest interconnect domain | Multi-terabyte embedding tables\index{DLRM!coordination bottleneck} exceed any device's memory, and live feature lookups demand random-access storage | Phone-class power, memory, and thermal envelopes\index{MobileNet!edge power envelope} cap what local training can attempt                                                                         |
| **Distribution (Part II)**    | 3D parallelism and AllReduce must fit the step budget, and Young-Daly checkpoint cadence tracks interruptions measured in hours                                                                                        | Embedding sharding turns lookups into AllToAll exchanges whose hottest receiver sets completion time                                                  | Federated averaging replaces AllReduce, and over-selection with round deadlines bounds the wait for intermittent clients                                                                          |
| **Serving (Part III)**        | Small-batch decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so batching, KV-cache policy, and lifetime serving cost shape deployment                                                                                              | Feature-parallel sharding and routing must hold tail latency within budget at millions of queries per second                                          | Adaptation runs only in admitted windows that preserve the foreground deadline, and rollouts span weeks of version skew                                                                           |
| **Governance (Part IV)**      | Data provenance, output leakage, and the energy of each training run gate release                                                                                                                                      | Recommendations shape future training data, requiring fairness and drift evidence with accountable response across the serving lifecycle              | Secure aggregation limits visibility of individual updates; differential privacy bounds released information under stated accounting assumptions; participation bias shapes whose data contribute |

: **Archetypes across the Fleet Stack**: The book's three running workloads traced through the four bands of the fleet stack, one band per part, beneath the representative binding C$^3$ term with which the introduction characterized each. The same Fleet Law applies to all three; the regimes shown here expose different constraints, not permanent bottleneck assignments. {#tbl-conclusion-archetype-binding-terms tbl-colwidths="[16,28,28,28]"}

Read down a column to trace the constraints one workload encounters across the bands; read across a row to compare how a band constrains different workloads. These constraints need not all bind at once. The representative terms describe operating regimes, not permanent assignments of archetypes to C$^3$ terms. Federated MobileNet can be device-compute-bound during local training yet communication- or coordination-bound during a global round with intermittent clients. The same six principles apply to all three; the engineer must measure the workload at the relevant boundary before choosing which term to reduce. Because the binding term must be found rather than assumed, the book's method reduces to a diagnostic procedure, a sequence of steps that is distinct from the principles it applies.

1. Start with the observed symptom, the user-visible or operator-visible failure.
2. Attach the metric that makes the symptom falsifiable.
3. Map the symptom to C$^3$ by identifying whether compute, communication, or coordination binds first.
4. Locate the fleet-stack row that owns the intervention.
5. State the cost that the proposed fix displaces elsewhere.
6. Preserve the audit, safety, security, or responsibility evidence needed to justify the decision.

On the expanded cluster, a training run that falls behind its schedule exercises every step of that procedure: the schedule lag is the symptom, and the falsifiable metric is model FLOPs utilization\index{Model FLOPs utilization!fleet diagnostic} measured per step, the measure of program goodput in @sec-performance-engineering-fleet-efficiency-metric-dff4, which has dropped since the expansion. A step profile shows accelerators idle at gradient-synchronization barriers, but that wait alone does not distinguish slow collective transfer from ranks arriving late after computation, data loading, or scheduling delays, so aligned per-rank traces must separate arrival skew from exposed collective completion time. When those traces show little arrival skew and increased exposed transfer time, they point to communication as the binding term and to the distributed-execution row, where the collective and its overlap are scheduled, as the owner of the intervention. A proposed fix such as gradient compression shrinks the exchanged bytes while displacing cost into convergence and accuracy risk, which means the evidence to preserve is the convergence and evaluation record showing that the compressed run still reaches its quality target. The same procedure redirects other symptoms: a fairness alert may point to missing labels, insufficient review capacity, or a serving-path threshold policy rather than model weights alone, and a security incident may point to artifact provenance, access permissions, or rollback evidence rather than network perimeter failure. The discipline is to follow the constraint until the row that owns it and the trade-off it carries are visible. When the fix changes what ships, the evidence from the final step enters the end-to-end evaluation contract\index{Evaluation contract!production release} (principle \ref{pri-evaluation-contract}), one versioned release record that binds the candidate to production-equivalent measurements, accountable acceptance authority, tested recovery, and explicit conditions that invalidate the evidence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The end-to-end evaluation contract and its versioned release record are established in @sec-ops-scale-end-to-end-evaluation-contract.
:::

## Competencies Mastered {#sec-conclusion-mastered-da67}

The proposed cluster expansion tests competence across the whole stack. Accepting it requires evidence that reduced compute time survives communication and recovery costs, while releasing its model requires a separate serving and governance judgment. Mastery means identifying those dependencies, choosing the measurements that test them, and defending the decision within the stated assumptions. Each band of the stack contributes one checkable part of that defense.

In the Infrastructure band, the governing question is which infrastructure limit binds the workload. An engineer who has mastered this material can match accelerator memory and compute to the model, provision storage and network bandwidth for the required rates, and account for power and cooling\index{Cooling!capacity constraint} as capacity constraints rather than facilities details. In the expansion, that skill decides whether the retained fabric, checkpoint tier, and site power can carry `{python} ConclusionExpansion.exp_gpus_str` at all.

In the Distribution band, the governing question is how to make a workload larger than any single machine behave as one coordinated system. An engineer can analyze communication patterns, select a parallelization strategy, and estimate failure cadence from component MTTF\index{MTTF!failure cadence}, fleet size, and the failure-dependence model. Given a collective's cost model, such as the Ring AllReduce\index{Ring AllReduce!bandwidth scaling} cost recalled under the second principle, the engineer can also predict which of its terms grows with $\DeviceCount$. In the expansion, this band produced the recovery estimate and the break-even speedup, and it identified exposed communication as the measurement that sets the price.

In the Serving band, the governing question is how a trained model keeps serving value under live traffic. An engineer can budget the serving tax\index{Serving tax!budgeting}, select batching and placement policies, and monitor system performance and input distributions in production so that a working model does not become an inefficient or stale service. In the expansion, this band decides whether the released model meets its latency contract with headroom left for recovery.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The serving tax that distributed execution adds to each request's latency budget is established in @sec-inference-scale-serving-tax-overhead-distribution-5ef3.
:::

In the Governance band, the governing question is who bears the costs and risks of the system's decisions. An engineer can translate security, privacy, fairness, robustness, and sustainability obligations into controls and evidence: access boundaries, privacy budgets\index{Privacy budget!differential privacy}, subgroup evaluations, adversarial, out-of-distribution, and concept-drift tests\index{Out-of-distribution robustness!testing}\index{Concept drift!monitoring}, incident procedures, and resource accounting. In the expansion, this band supplies the security, subgroup, and carbon evidence that the release decision requires. These competencies connect model development to the consequences of deployment. They also supply a test of transfer. When a new workload or substrate appears, the engineer must identify its accounting boundary, constraints, and evidence requirements before accepting an efficiency claim.

## Where the Binding Constraint Moves Next {#sec-conclusion-path-forward-caa2}

When a reasoning model spends seconds of test-time compute on a single user prompt or thousands of accelerators burn link power on every Mixture-of-Experts AllToAll dispatch, the binding constraint shifts again without leaving the Fleet Law behind. The same six principles apply to workloads and substrates that are only now emerging. Test-time compute, introduced among the scaling regimes in @sec-vol2-intro-resourceconstrained-scaling-regimes-062d, already moves part of the scaling curve from the training cluster into the serving path, where @sec-inference-logic-wall prices it as a per-request compute budget. Beneath the fleet, new interconnect and packaging substrates change the rates that every Fleet Law term inherits. Each shift relocates cost without exempting it from the Fleet Law.

Gains from scheduling, placement, and overlap depend on a physical fabric, so software and substrate choices must be evaluated together. Once software has removed avoidable coordination, the remaining frontier is the substrate that moves tokens, activations, and power through the fleet. For Archetype A, the pressure on that substrate comes from specific collective patterns rather than from scale in general. Tensor parallelism\index{Tensor parallelism!collective communication} issues frequent collectives across partitioned tensors, and mixture-of-experts (MoE)\index{MoE!AllToAll routing} routing issues an AllToAll dispatch at each expert layer. Across thousands of accelerators, link energy accumulates with the volume of that collective traffic, which makes lower-energy interconnects a plausible fabric-efficiency lever.

The candidates are substrates the book has already met. Optical I/O\index{Optical interconnect!optical I/O} and co-packaged optics\index{Optical interconnect!co-packaged optics} entered with the network fabric as ways to lower energy per bit, 3D integration\index{3D integration!bandwidth density} extends the stacking that HBM and advanced packaging already use to shorten connections, and neuromorphic event-driven substrates\index{Neuromorphic computing!event-driven substrates}\index{Non-von Neumann computing!neuromorphic substrates} appeared among the research directions for sustainable fleets as a way to organize computation around sparse events such as spikes and keep state beside the compute that uses it. Each attacks a different factor of the same account: energy per bit, path length, bandwidth density, or the distance between memory and compute. Automated architecture search and AI-for-systems optimization\index{Hardware-software co-design!AI for systems} offer ways to explore candidate designs, but each proposal still needs a workload-specific comparison of useful work, data movement, power, and implementation cost. A lower energy per bit also reaches the fleet only in proportion to the links' share of fleet power, the affected-share arithmetic of Amdahl's law applied to energy, so its value is measured as that share, as the optical dividend of @sec-network-fabrics-optical does for a switch and a cluster. A lower link-energy measurement alone therefore does not establish a better fleet, and a new substrate still needs fault tolerance and responsible governance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Neuromorphic and other non-von Neumann directions are established in @sec-sustainable-ai-future-challenges-58e2.
:::

Whatever the substrate, the discipline stays the same. An engineer chooses the unit of useful work, accounts for its full resource cost, and states which comparisons the evidence supports.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-conclusion-fallacies-pitfalls}

The closing mistakes all come from optimizing the wrong unit of design. A model can improve while the fleet becomes slower, less reliable, more expensive, or harder to govern.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A faster model is automatically a better system.*

Raw model speed matters, but it is only one term in the Fleet Law. In the illustrative equal-work, barrier-dominated step, a worker running at `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.straggler_speed_pct_str` of peer speed reduces throughput by `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.straggler_drop_pct_str` relative to uniformly fast workers. A faster kernel on every worker but that one leaves the step bound by the straggler, because speeding the workers already waiting at the barrier does not shorten the limiting computation. A design that reduces kernel time while increasing checkpoint pressure, network contention, serving variance, or governance risk can make the total system worse. The systems question is whether the change improves useful throughput\index{Goodput!useful throughput}, the ML goodput of @sec-performance-engineering-measurement-scale, under the actual constraints: data movement, synchronization, failure recovery, power, latency, and accountability.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Optimizing one layer while hiding the constraint it creates in another.*

A local improvement becomes dangerous when it moves cost to a layer that no one is measuring: larger batches may raise accelerator utilization while worsening tail latency, aggressive compression may reduce communication while increasing accuracy risk, and carbon-aware scheduling may lower emissions while requiring more slack in the service budget. Good engineering respects the displacement of overhead\index{Displacement of overhead!cross-layer optimization}, keeping the transferred constraint visible so the system can choose deliberately rather than inheriting a hidden bottleneck.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Fleet-scale lessons are tied to today's hardware and software stack.*

Specific processors, frameworks, and serving engines will change, but the durable relationships remain: data must reach compute at the required rate, workers must communicate before synchronization stalls the job, failures must be expected at large component counts, serving systems must meet tail-latency budgets, and governance constraints must be engineered into the operating path. The technology names are examples; the rate, failure, and accountability relationships are the lesson.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating governance and sustainability as external reviews rather than system constraints.*

Postponing security, fairness, privacy, and carbon accounting can create architectural debt\index{Architectural debt!delayed governance}. Retrofitting audit trails, demographic monitoring, access controls, deletion workflows, or carbon-aware placement may require reconstructing evidence or redesigning deployed components. Identifying these obligations during design lets teams budget the required paths and test whether they work before release; the actual cost still depends on the control and deployment.

:::

## Summary {#sec-conclusion-summary}

At fleet scale, improving a model or accelerator does not establish that the complete service improves. The engineering object is the coupled system that moves data, schedules work, survives failure, serves users, and satisfies governance obligations under physical and organizational constraints. Within their fitted regime, scaling laws set the demand for fleet growth, the Fleet Law sets its price, and the six principles locate where in the fleet that price is paid. The method that recurs across the book follows from all three. It identifies the binding constraint, quantifies its cost, and evaluates the proposed change across every affected operating path, so that the cost it displaces stays visible instead of resurfacing unmeasured in another layer.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="The fleet is the unit of design"}

* **The fleet is the object**: The volume's six principles reduce to one habit, following the binding constraint\index{Binding constraint!cross-layer analysis} across infrastructure, communication, coordination, serving, and governance. The fleet, not any single model or component, is the unit to build, measure, and optimize.
* **Growth must earn its price**: Within a fitted regime, each doubling of compute buys a smaller absolute loss reduction, while interruption exposure and checkpoint overhead grow with the fleet and exposed communication can grow with it. Expansion is a decision justified by measurements and release evidence, not a default.
* **Scale changes the probability model**: When server delays are independent, a request that touches `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_servers_str` has a `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_hit_pct_str` chance that at least one responds beyond its `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.tail_percentile_str`th-percentile latency, and a job that needs every one of $\RequiredComponentCount$ independent components sees its interval between interruptions shrink as $1/\RequiredComponentCount$. Fleet behavior is not single-node behavior repeated.
* **Orchestration gains require system measurements**: Scheduling, placement, and communication overlap\index{Orchestration!efficiency gains} improve useful throughput only when their gains survive recovery costs, serving deadlines, and resource budgets. Measure the complete operating path before accepting a local improvement as a fleet-wide gain.
* **Obligations belong in the path**: Security, privacy, fairness, robustness, carbon, and auditability are production constraints\index{Governance!operating path integration}, not external reviews. The discipline is to design them into data pipelines, schedulers, serving paths, and operating procedures before scale makes the trade-off irreversible.

:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection label="Closing Distillation" title="The discipline of ML systems"}

@Sec-vol2-introduction-scale-moment traced the scale moment through a training run that stopped every few hours. Meta's Llama 3 cluster of `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_gpus_str` GPUs recorded `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_failures_str` in `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_days_str` and still kept more than `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_effective_pct_str` of elapsed time as useful training [@dubey2024llama]. Those numbers now read as engineering. An unexpected interruption every `{python} ConclusionScaleFacts.llama_hours_per_failure_str` is the reliability gap of a job that needs every one of its accelerators at once, and it measures the run's recovery exposure; the effective training fraction, the run's runtime goodput, measures how much progress the recovery machinery retained across elapsed time. The report credits faster startup, checkpointing, and diagnosis, including communication traces that made stalled collectives inspectable, for that retained fraction, so the fraction summarizes all of them together rather than measuring any single Fleet Law term. Each worker still computed, exchanged, and waited, as in the synchronous step with which the book began; Compute, Communication, and Coordination are those three activities, measured.

A proposed larger run can now be judged rather than presumed necessary. Under the expansion example's independent, identical constant-rate failure model and unchanged checkpoint write time, doubling the fleet halves the expected interruption interval and raises optimized checkpoint-and-rework overhead by about `{python} ConclusionExpansion.ckpt_overhead_growth_mult_str`, and it buys calendar time only by spending more accelerator-hours on the same work. Whether that run should be built depends on the shrinking quality gain its fitted scaling curve predicts for the doubling, the measured time and energy required to deliver it, and the evidence its release requires. The engineering achievement is a justified decision, including the decision to retain the current fleet when expansion cannot meet those conditions. The same discipline applies whether the work scales training compute across thousands of accelerators or serves a model to millions of users under a latency contract. The engineer follows the binding constraint across the fleet, accounts for every displaced cost, and accepts a design only when the evidence supports it.

:::

*Prof. Vijay Janapa Reddi, Harvard University*
